questions.question: The Supreme Court of India comprises the Chief Justice and not more than _______ other Judges appointed by the President of India.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**33**__.

__
 
• The Supreme Court of India consists of the Chief Justice of India and not more than 33 other Judges.
 
• These Judges are appointed by the President of India.
 
• The maximum number of Judges in the Supreme Court is defined under Article 124 of the Indian Constitution.
 
• This number can be increased by Parliament through legislation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• The Chief Justice of India is the head of the judiciary system in India.
 
• The CJI is appointed by the President of India based on seniority and other considerations.
 
• The CJI plays a crucial role in the administration of justice and is responsible for the allocation of cases and appointment of constitutional benches.
 
 
 
• **Appointment of Judges**
 
 
• Judges of the Supreme Court are appointed by the President of India under Article 124(2) of the Constitution of India.
 
• The appointment process involves consultation with the Chief Justice of India and other senior judges.
 
• Once appointed, judges can serve until the age of 65.
 
 
 
• **Article 124 of the Indian Constitution**
 
 
• Article 124 of the Indian Constitution deals with the establishment and constitution of the Supreme Court.
 
• It outlines the appointment, tenure, and removal of Supreme Court judges.
 
• It also provides for the Parliament's power to increase the number of judges through legislation.
 
 
 
• **Parliament's Power**
 
 
• The Parliament of India has the authority to change the number of judges in the Supreme Court through legislation.
 
• This ensures that the judiciary can be expanded to meet the needs of a growing nation.
 
• The number of judges has been increased several times since the establishment of the Supreme Court to handle the increasing workload.

questions.question: How many times has the term judicial review been mentioned in the constitution?
questions.solution:

• The Judicial review system in Indian Constitution is taken from the United States of America.
 
• The power of the Judicial Review is declared as part of the basic structure of the Indian Constitution by the Supreme Court in the Indira Gandhi vs Raj Narain Case 1975.
 
• The judicial review is the process of scrutinizing any decision or law made by the government, by the courts of the country.
 
• The term judicial review is not mentioned in the constitution of India

questions.question: What is the sanctioned judge strength of the Supreme Court excluding Chief Justice of India as per the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act, 2019?

• As a result, the date of establishment is considered official.

• It is the highest-ranking constitutional court with judicial review authority.

questions.question: A judge of the Supreme Court can be removed only on the grounds of ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**proven misbehaviour or incapacity**__.

__
 
• A **judge of the Supreme Court **can be** removed only on the grounds of proven misbehaviour or incapacity**.
 
• An **order of the President must be passed** after an address in **each House of Parliament,** **supported by a majority of the members present and voting and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of those present and voting, and presented to the President in the same Session** for such removal on the ground of such proven misbehavior or incapacity.
 
• Otherwise, a judge of the Supreme Court cannot be removed from office. The **practice of law in any court **or before any other body in India** is prohibited for anyone who has served as a judge of the Supreme Court.**

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] Additional Information__**

 
• ​The **process for removal judges is outlined in Article 124(4)** of the Indian Constitution. The **President must issue an order** before removing a **Supreme Court Judge** from office.
 
• The **consent of both Houses of Parliament is required** for such an order. It needs a particular majority of the members who are present and voting within the same session.
 
• The **criteria for **removal a**re proven misconduct or incompetence**. After giving notice to the **Speaker or Chairman of the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha**, respectively, it comes to light.
 
• A **three-judge panel conducts a thorough examination**. They **present the report during the following joint session** of both Houses of Parliament.

• The **President of India** appoints an **Acting Chief Justice** in the absence of the **Chief Justice of India (CJI).**
 
• This provision is made under **Article 126** of the **Indian Constitution**, which deals with the designation of an Acting Chief Justice.
 
• The **Acting Chief Justice** is usually the **senior-most judge** of the **Supreme Court**, ensuring continuity in the judiciary's functioning.
 
• The appointment is essential to ensure that the **Supreme Court** functions smoothly even in the absence of the **CJI**.

questions.question: Which Article of the Constitution of India declares the Supreme Court to be a court of record?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 129**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Article 129 of the Constitution of India declares the Supreme Court to be a court of record.
 
• This means that the Supreme Court’s judgments, proceedings, and acts are recorded for perpetual memory and testimony.
 
• The records of the Supreme Court have evidentiary value and cannot be questioned when produced before any court.
 
• As a court of record, the Supreme Court has the power to punish for contempt of court, either with simple imprisonment or with a fine.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 126:**

 
 
• This article deals with the appointment of an acting Chief Justice of India.
 
• It states that when the office of Chief Justice of India is vacant or when the Chief Justice is unable to perform duties, the President can appoint an acting Chief Justice from among the judges of the Supreme Court.
 
 
 
• **Article 128:**
 
 
• This article allows for the attendance of retired judges at sittings of the Supreme Court.
 
• It states that the Chief Justice of India, with the prior consent of the President, can request any retired judge of the Supreme Court or a High Court to act as a judge of the Supreme Court for a temporary period.
 
 
 
• **Article 125:**
 
 
• This article deals with the salaries, allowances, leave of absence, pensions, etc., of the judges of the Supreme Court.
 
• It ensures that the judges receive such emoluments and privileges as determined by Parliament by law, and until so determined, as specified in the Second Schedule of the Constitution.

questions.question: In which of the following years was the Bombay High Court of India established?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1862**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Bombay High Court, one of the oldest High Courts in India, was established on **August 14, 1862**.
 
• It was established under the **Indian High Courts Act of 1861** by Queen Victoria.
 
• The jurisdiction of the Bombay High Court extends to the states of Maharashtra, Goa, and the Union Territories of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu.
 
• The court has its principal seat in Mumbai (Bombay) and benches at Nagpur, Aurangabad, and Panaji (Goa).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indian High Courts Act of 1861**

 
 
• The Indian High Courts Act of 1861 was an Act of the Parliament of the United Kingdom to establish High Courts in India.
 
• The Act authorized the British Crown to establish High Courts in the presidencies of Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras.
 
• The Act abolished the Supreme Courts at Calcutta, Madras, and Bombay and the Sadar Adalats in Presidency towns, merging their jurisdictions to form the High Courts.
 
• The High Courts were given the power to exercise original and appellate jurisdiction in civil and criminal cases.
 
 
 
• **Bombay High Court**
 
 
• The Bombay High Court is renowned for its rich heritage and historical significance.
 
• It has played a pivotal role in the development of Indian jurisprudence and has a long-standing tradition of delivering landmark judgments.
 
• The architectural design of the court building is a blend of Gothic and early English styles, symbolizing the legacy of British colonial rule in India.
 
• Prominent judges and lawyers, including Dr. B.R. Ambedkar and Nani Palkhivala, have been associated with the Bombay High Court.
 
 
 
• **Judicial System in India**
 
 
• The judicial system in India is a hierarchical system with the Supreme Court at the top, followed by High Courts at the state level, and subordinate courts at the district and lower levels.
 
• High Courts have the power to hear appeals from lower courts and have original jurisdiction in certain matters.
 
• The Indian judiciary is independent of the executive and legislative branches of government, ensuring the rule of law and protection of fundamental rights.
 
• Judicial review is a key function of the judiciary, allowing courts to examine the constitutionality of legislative and executive actions.

questions.question: Which is NOT correct about the independence of the judiciary in our country?

options.text: The judiciary has the power to penalise those who are found guilty of contempt of court.
The judges are financially dependent on both the executive and legislature for their salaries and allowances.
The Constitution prescribes a very difficult procedure for removal of judges.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The judges are financially dependent on both the executive and legislature for their salaries and allowances.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points**__

 
• Independence of the judiciary means that the other organs of the government like the executive and legislature must not restrain the functioning of the judiciary in such a way that it is unable to do justice.
 
• judges must be able to perform their functions without fear or favor. 
 
• The Indian Constitution has ensured the independence of the judiciary through a number of measures.
 
• The legislature is not involved in the process of appointment of judges. Hence option 4 is correct. 
 
 
• Thus, it was believed that party politics would not play a role in the process of appointments.
 
• In order to be appointed as a judge, a person must have experience as a lawyer and/or must be well-versed in the law.
 
• The judges have a fixed tenure. 
 
 
• They hold office till reaching the age of retirement.
 
• Only in exceptional cases, judges may be removed.
 
• Security of tenure ensures that judges could function without fear or favor.
 
• The Constitution makers believed that a difficult procedure of removal would provide security of office to the members of the judiciary. **Hence option 3 is correct.**
 
 
 
• The judiciary is not financially dependent on either the executive or legislature. Hence option 2 is not correct. 
 
 
• The Constitution provides that the salaries and allowances of the judges are not subjected to the approval of the legislature.
 
• The actions and decisions of the judges are immune from personal criticism.
 
 
 
• The judiciary has the power to penalize those who are found guilty of contempt of court. Hence Option 1 is correct. 
 
 
• Parliament cannot discuss the conduct of the judges except when the proceeding to remove a judge is being carried out.
 
• This gives the judiciary independence to adjudicate without fear of being criticized.

questions.question: The _______ repeals the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC).
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita Bill**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The Indian Lok Sabha recently passed the Bharatiya Nyaya (Second) Sanhita, 2023 bill to replace the Indian Penal Code (IPC) of 1860. The new bill has included a provision for the death penalty for those guilty of mob lynching.
 
• According to Section 103 (2) of the new bill, any group of five or more persons found guilty of committing murder on the ground of race, caste, community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief, or any similar ground will face the punishment of death or life imprisonment, in addition to other potential fines.
 
• Union Home Minister Amit Shah has stated in the Lok Sabha that mob lynching is a grave crime, and, in order to deter this practice, the death penalty provision has been included in the new laws.
 
• The new bill has also introduced a specific chapter titled 'Crimes against Women and Children', focusing on sexual crimes. It includes severe punishment for gang rape, with a minimum of 20 years of imprisonment or life sentence being mandated.
 
• The term 'sedition' has been completely removed from the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita Bill. The new legislation, instead, introduces the term 'treason' with focus on acts that endanger 'sovereignty or unity and integrity of India'. The definition of treason includes the mention of 'intent', providing a safeguard for freedom of expression.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The bill further modifies certain language to better represent its legal intentions. Words such as 'hatred' and 'contempt' have been removed and phrases like 'armed rebellion', 'destructive activities', and 'separatist activities' have been included.
 
• Overall, the new Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita includes 358 sections compared to the previous 511 in the IPC.
 
• It adds 21 new offences, increases imprisonment terms for 41 offences, enhances penalties for 82 offences, introduces minimum mandatory punishment for 25 crimes, includes community service as a punishment in 6 crimes, and repeals 19 sections.

questions.question: Which of the following state High Court's jurisdiction extends to the Union Territories of Daman and Diu?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Bombay High Court**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Bombay High Court has jurisdiction over the state of Maharashtra and the Union Territories of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu.
 
• It was one of the three High Courts in India established at the Presidency towns by the Letters patent granted by Her Majesty Queen Victoria, bearing date June 26, 1862.
 
• The High Court is located in Mumbai, the capital city of Maharashtra.
 
• The court has regional branches at Nagpur, Aurangabad, and Panaji (Goa).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **High Courts in India**

 
 
• India has a high court in each state and union territory, although some high courts have jurisdiction over more than one state or union territory.
 
• High Courts are the principal civil courts of original jurisdiction in each state and union territory, and they are empowered to hear both civil and criminal matters.
 
• They also have the power to hear appeals from lower courts and to issue writs for enforcing fundamental rights.
 
• The judges of the High Courts are appointed by the President of India in consultation with the Chief Justice of India and the governor of the state.
 
 
 
• **Union Territories of Daman and Diu**
 
 
• Daman and Diu were two separate districts of the union territory of Daman and Diu until 2019.
 
• In 2020, they were merged with Dadra and Nagar Haveli to form the new union territory of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu.
 
• These territories were part of Portuguese India until they were annexed by India in 1961.
 
• The High Court with jurisdiction over these territories is the Bombay High Court.
 
 
 
• **Jurisdiction**
 
 
• Jurisdiction refers to the official power to make legal decisions and judgments.
 
• In the context of High Courts, it refers to the geographic area or the range of cases over which the court has authority.
 
• Some High Courts have jurisdiction over multiple states or union territories, while others are limited to a single state or union territory.
 
• The jurisdiction of a High Court can be extended or altered by legislation.

questions.question: The jurisdiction of the Supreme Court is guaranteed by the:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Constitution**__.

__
 
• The jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in India is explicitly outlined and guaranteed by the **Constitution of India**.
 
• It derives its authority from **Articles 124 to 147** of the Constitution, which detail its powers, functions, and responsibilities.
 
• The Supreme Court has **original jurisdiction, appellate jurisdiction, and advisory jurisdiction** as per the Constitution.
 
• It serves as the guardian of the Constitution and ensures the protection of fundamental rights under Part III of the Constitution.
 
• The independence and functioning of the Supreme Court are safeguarded to uphold the principle of **separation of powers** and judicial autonomy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Original Jurisdiction:** The Supreme Court has exclusive jurisdiction in cases involving disputes between the Union and states or between states, as per Article 131.
 
• **Appellate Jurisdiction:** It allows the Supreme Court to hear appeals in constitutional, civil, and criminal cases from lower courts, under Articles 132, 133, and 134.
 
• **Advisory Jurisdiction:** As per Article 143, the President of India can seek the Supreme Court's opinion on matters of public importance or constitutional interpretation.
 
• **Judicial Review:** The Supreme Court ensures the constitutionality of laws and executive actions through judicial review, a key feature of the Indian Constitution.
 
• **Public Interest Litigation (PIL):** The Supreme Court allows citizens to file PILs to address issues of public concern, ensuring greater access to justice.

• **Entry of women to Sabarimala:- **

 
 
• The Supreme Court on 28 September 2018 allowed entry of women of all ages into the Ayyappa temple at Sabarimala in Kerala.
 
• The SC said banning entry of women to Kerala's Sabarimala temple is gender discrimination and the practice violates rights of Hindu women.
 
• **Justice Indu Malhotra penned a dissenting opinion Entry of women to Sabarimala. **

• **Doctrine of Basic Structure:-**

 
 
• It is a judicial principle developed by the Supreme Court of India in 1973.
 
• This principle emerged in the Keshavananda Bharati judgment.
 
• The Parliament of India is vested with the power of amending the Constitution (Article 368). But, the doctrine of basic structure restricts the powers of the Parliament.
 
• According to this, the Supreme Court has the power to declare any law void if it is found to be unconstitutional.
 
• Any amendment that tries to change the basic structure of the constitution is considered unconstitutional, though the term ';basic structure' is not mentioned in the constitution and has evolved over time.
 
• This principle thus helps to protect and preserve the spirit of the constitution document.

• It **formed a National Judicial Appointments Commission.**

• **​**The **82nd Amendment Act of the Indian Constitution** (2000) introduced a crucial provision to protect the interests of the Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs) in matters of employment. 
 
• The amendment added a **proviso to Article 335 of the Constitution**.
 
• **Article 335 originally states that the claims of SCs and STs** must be taken into consideration in appointments to services and posts, while ensuring the maintenance of efficiency in administration.
 
• The **amendment allowed the government to relax qualifying marks and standards of evaluation for SCs and STs i**n matters of reservation in promotions.
 
 
 
• **52nd Amendment Act**
 
 
• The **52nd Amendment Act of the Indian Constitution** (1985) is a landmark legislation known for introducing the **anti-defection law**.
 
• The amendment added the **Tenth Schedule to the Constitution,** commonly referred to as the Anti-Defection Law.
 
• It **aims to curb political defections by members of the legislature**, which were seen as undermining the stability of governments and the principles of democracy.** **

• The Supreme Court of India has **Exclusive Original Jurisdiction** in any dispute between the Government of India and one or more States or between the Government of India and any State or States.
 
• This jurisdiction is exclusive, meaning that no other court can hear these types of disputes.
 
• Under Article 131 of the Indian Constitution, the Supreme Court has the power to adjudicate in disputes involving the Government of India and States.
 
• Exclusive Original Jurisdiction ensures that such disputes are resolved at the highest level of the judiciary, maintaining the balance and sovereignty of the federal structure.

• **Advisory Jurisdiction**

 
 
• Under Article 143 of the Indian Constitution, the President of India can refer any question of law or fact to the Supreme Court for its opinion.
 
• The advisory opinion given by the Supreme Court is not binding.
 
 
 
• **Appellate Jurisdiction**
 
 
• Under this jurisdiction, the Supreme Court hears appeals against the judgments of lower courts (High Courts) in civil, criminal, and constitutional matters.
 
• Articles 132, 133, and 134 of the Constitution deal with the appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.
 
 
 
• **Writ Jurisdiction**
 
 
• Under Article 32 of the Indian Constitution, the Supreme Court can issue writs to enforce the fundamental rights of individuals.
 
• The writs include Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Quo-Warranto, and Certiorari.

questions.question: In which year was the first-ever motion to remove a Supreme Court Justice signed by the members of Parliament?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1991**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The first-ever motion to remove a Supreme Court Justice in India was signed in **1991**.
 
• The motion was targeted at Justice V. Ramaswami, who faced allegations of financial irregularities.
 
• The motion was initiated by the then Law Minister Subramanian Swamy.
 
• The process led to the formation of a three-member judicial committee to investigate the charges.
 
• Although the committee found him guilty, the motion did not pass in the Lok Sabha due to lack of requisite majority.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Impeachment Process of Judges**

 
 
• The procedure for the removal of judges is outlined in Article 124(4) and Article 217 of the Indian Constitution.
 
• A judge can be removed on grounds of proven misbehavior or incapacity.
 
• The process can be initiated in either House of Parliament.
 
• The motion needs to be supported by a specified number of members before it can be admitted.
 
 
 
• **Judicial Committee**
 
 
• Once the motion is admitted, a three-member committee investigates the charges.
 
• The committee consists of a Supreme Court judge, a Chief Justice of a High Court, and a distinguished jurist.
 
 
 
• **Final Decision**
 
 
• If the committee finds the judge guilty, the House can take up the motion for debate and voting.
 
• The motion must be passed by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting in each House of Parliament.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context**
 
 
• Justice V. Ramaswami was the first Supreme Court judge to face an impeachment motion.
 
• The case highlighted the need for transparency and accountability in the judiciary.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT regarding the collegium system?

options.text: This system started in the year 2007.
This system was evolved through Supreme Court judgment.
It recommends the appointments and transfers of judges.
It consists of Chief Justice and four senior judges of Supreme Court.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**This system started in the year 2007. **__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• This system started in the year 2007.
 
• **This is Incorrect**: The collegium system did not start in 2007.
 
 
• It evolved through judicial decisions in three landmark cases known as the **Three Judges Cases**:
 
 
• **First Judges Case (1981):** The executive had primacy in judicial appointments.
 
• **Second Judges Case (1993):** The judiciary established its primacy by creating the collegium system for judicial appointments.
 
• **Third Judges Case (1998):** Expanded the collegium to include the Chief Justice of India (CJI) and **four senior-most judges** of the Supreme Court.
 
 
 
• Thus, the collegium system became functional in **1993**, not 2007.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

Collegium system:

 
• It is the system of appointment and transfer of judges that has evolved through judgments of the Supreme Court, and not by an Act of Parliament or by a provision of the Constitution.
 
• The Supreme Court collegium is headed by the CJI (Chief Justice of India) and comprises four other senior-most judges of the court.
 
• Judges of the higher judiciary are appointed only through the collegium system and the government has a role only after names have been decided by the collegium.

questions.question: The State of Kerala Vs Leesamma Joseph case deals with ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**persons with disabilities.**__

__
 
• ** State of Kerala Vs Leesamma Joseph:-**

 
 
• The Supreme Court of India in its judgment on 28 June 2021 in the case of "State of Kerala vs Leesamma Joseph" affirmed that persons with disabilities have a right to reservation in promotion under Article 16(4) of the Constitution of India, 1950.
 
• While examining the constitutionality of Section 33 of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, the Court noted that 'equality of opportunity' in matters of public employment includes provision of certain reservations in favour of persons with disabilities.
 
• Furthermore, it held that Article 16(4) of the Constitution, empowering the State to make provisions for reservation in matters of promotion in favour of any backward class of citizens, also includes persons with disabilities within its scope, regardless of the nature of their establishments, whether they belong to the public sector or the private sector.

• This is the principal legislation that protects the rights of individuals with disabilities in India.
 
• It replaces and strengthens the Persons with Disabilities Act, 1995.
 
• The RPDA complies with the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, to which India is a signatory.
 
• The Act expands the list of recognized disabilities from 7 to 21, and mandates the central and state governments to take measures to ensure that persons with disabilities fully enjoy all human rights and fundamental freedoms.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements are correct regarding the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of India?

A. Original jurisdiction extends to any dispute between the Government of India and one or more States or between the Government of India and any State or States on one side and one or more States on the other or between two or more States.

B. Appellate Jurisdiction extends when the Union plus some States are one side and some other States on the other side of the dispute.

C. Under Articles 129 and 142 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court has been vested with the power to punish for contempt of court.

D. As of now, the International Commercial Arbitration cannot be initiated in the Supreme Court.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**3) A and C only**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

The Supreme Court's original jurisdiction extends to any dispute between the Government of India and one or more States or between the Government of India and any State or States on one side and one or more States on the other or between two or more States.
 
• **Contempt of Court:** Statement C is also correct. Under Articles 129 and 142 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court has been vested with the power to punish for contempt of court.
 
• Statement B is incorrect because the appellate jurisdiction does not extend to disputes where the Union and some States are on one side and other States are on the other side.
 
• Statement D is incorrect as the Supreme Court can entertain international commercial arbitration matters under its jurisdiction.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The Supreme Court of India is the highest judicial forum and final court of appeal under the Constitution of India.
 
• It has extensive powers in the form of original, appellate, and advisory jurisdictions.
 
• The Supreme Court's decisions are binding on all other courts within the territory of India.
 
• The Supreme Court can also transfer cases from one High Court to another and even from one subordinate court to another in the interest of justice.

questions.question: Which article empowers the Supreme Court to exercise the jurisdiction and powers of the federal court under any pre-constitution law?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 135**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Article 135** of the Indian Constitution empowers the Supreme Court to exercise the jurisdiction and powers of a federal court under any pre-constitution law in certain cases.
 
• This provision ensures that the Supreme Court retains jurisdiction in matters where powers were exercised by the Federal Court of India before the Constitution came into effect.
 
• The Federal Court of India, established under the **Government of India Act, 1935**, was a precursor to the Supreme Court of India.
 
• Article 135 allows the Supreme Court to hear cases related to pre-constitutional laws until they are repealed or amended by Parliament.
 
• This article plays a crucial role in ensuring continuity and stability in India’s legal framework during the transition from colonial to independent governance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Federal Court of India (1937-1950):**

 
 
• It was established under the Government of India Act, 1935, to resolve disputes between provinces and hear appeals against decisions of the High Courts.
 
• The Federal Court was replaced by the Supreme Court of India upon the adoption of the Constitution in 1950.
 
 
 
• **Government of India Act, 1935:**
 
 
• It was a significant constitutional reform by the British Parliament that served as a blueprint for India’s federal structure.
 
• It introduced provincial autonomy and a federal court system in British India.
 
 
 
• **Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court:**
 
 
• The Supreme Court has original, appellate, and advisory jurisdiction under Articles 131-136 and Article 143 of the Constitution.
 
• Article 135 complements these powers by extending the Court’s jurisdiction over pre-constitutional legal matters.
 
 
 
• **Continuity of Legal Framework:**
 
 
• Article 372 of the Constitution also ensures that laws in force before the adoption of the Constitution continue unless repealed or amended.
 
• In combination with Article 135, this ensures seamless legal continuity during India’s transition to constitutional democracy.
